cls: Nonionic, low-osmolar iodinated radiographic contrast agent (radiopaque diagnostic medium)
pharm: Water-soluble nonionic tri-iodinated contrast agent (Ultravist) whose covalently bound iodine atoms attenuate X-rays (photon attenuation) in proportion to concentration, opacifying vessels and tissues for angiography, urography, and contrast-enhanced CT; dosed by iodine concentration (mgI/mL) and procedure, distributed extracellularly, and excreted ~97% unchanged by the kidneys.
quick: By concentration (mgI/mL) and procedure, e.g. coronary 370 mgI/mL 3-14 mL/injection, left ventricle 30-60 mL, CT head/body 50-200 mL, urography ~300 mgI/kg
Not applicable - single procedural intravascular diagnostic agent
Category B; animal studies show no teratogenicity; use only if clearly needed
Poorly excreted in milk; may continue nursing or pump and discard for 12-24 hours
Major concern - contrast-induced AKI; use lowest dose, hydrate, monitor eGFR; half-life prolonged in impairment; dialyzable
Excreted unchanged renally; hepatic impairment has limited effect on elimination
Not applicable to the agent; relevant only as a factor in metformin withholding
Renal function/eGFR before and after, hydration, 30-60 min hypersensitivity observation, vital signs, injection site
summary: Iopromide (Ultravist) is a nonionic, low-osmolar iodinated radiographic contrast agent for intravenous and intra-arterial use whose iodine attenuates X-rays to opacify vessels and tissues. It is supplied by iodine concentration in mgI/mL (historically 150, 240, 300, 370; the current label centers on 300 and 370), with concentration chosen by procedure - 370 for coronary/visceral/ventriculography, 300 for cerebral/peripheral arteriography, urography, and CT. The principal safety concerns are acute kidney injury / contrast-induced nephropathy (use the lowest dose and hydrate before and after), life-threatening anaphylactoid/hypersensitivity reactions (prior reaction triples the risk; have resuscitation equipment ready and observe 30-60 minutes), cardiovascular and thromboembolic events during arterial procedures, extravasation tissue injury, and thyroid effects. Ultravist must NOT be given intrathecally - inadvertent intrathecal administration can cause death, seizures, and severe neurologic injury. Metformin is managed around the procedure to avoid lactic acidosis if AKI occurs.
indications: Intra-arterial (adults): cerebral arteriography and peripheral arteriography (300 mgI/mL); coronary arteriography, left ventriculography, visceral angiography, and aortography (370 mgI/mL)
Intra-arterial (pediatric >=2 years): radiographic evaluation of the cardiac chambers and related arteries (370 mgI/mL)
Intravenous (adults and pediatric >=2 years): excretory urography and contrast-enhanced CT of the head and body
Historical additional concentrations: intra-arterial digital subtraction angiography (150 mgI/mL) and peripheral venography (240 mgI/mL)

admin: Use aseptic technique; inspect for particulates and discoloration; do not mix with other drugs in the same syringe or line
May be warmed to body temperature before use to improve comfort and reduce viscosity
Choose concentration and volume by procedure, vessel, blood flow, age, weight, and renal status - use the lowest dose that achieves adequate imaging
Hydrate the patient adequately before and after administration
Always have emergency resuscitation equipment and trained personnel immediately available; observe the patient for 30-60 minutes after dosing
Do NOT administer intrathecally; for arterial procedures use meticulous catheter technique with frequent heparinized-saline flushing to limit thromboembolic events
moa: Iopromide is a nonionic, water-soluble, tri-iodinated contrast agent. After intravascular injection its covalently bound iodine atoms attenuate (absorb) X-ray photons in direct proportion to the local iodine concentration, increasing the radiographic density of the blood, vessels, and perfused or excreting tissues relative to surrounding structures and thereby producing diagnostic opacification. It distributes rapidly into the extracellular (interstitial) space, can cross a disrupted blood-brain barrier, and is pharmacologically inert. Being nonionic, it does not dissociate into ions and has lower osmolality than older ionic high-osmolar agents at equivalent iodine content, reducing osmotic adverse effects. Protein binding is negligible (~1%) and it is excreted essentially unchanged (~97%) in the urine by glomerular filtration.

absolute: Intrathecal administration (risk of death, convulsions, cerebral hemorrhage, coma, paralysis, arachnoiditis, acute renal failure, cardiac arrest)
Preparatory dehydration before administration in pediatric patients (risk of acute renal failure)
Known severe/anaphylactoid hypersensitivity to iopromide (current FDA labeling lists Contraindications as None, but a prior severe reaction is a practical hard stop)
relative: Prior reaction to contrast media (about 3-fold increased risk), known iodine sensitivity, asthma, hay fever, or food allergy (about 2-fold)
Pre-existing renal impairment, diabetes, multiple myeloma/paraproteinemia, advanced vascular disease, or dehydration (contrast-induced AKI)
Congestive heart failure and severe coronary or cardiac disease
Hyperthyroidism or thyroid autonomy; pheochromocytoma; homozygous sickle cell disease
Severe arterial or venous disease at the injection site (extravasation risk)
monitor: Renal function (serum creatinine / eGFR) before and after the procedure
Hypersensitivity/anaphylactoid reactions, observing for 30-60 minutes after dosing
Vital signs and cardiovascular status during and after arterial procedures
Thyroid function in pediatric patients 0-3 years

preg: Pregnancy Category B. Reproduction studies in rats and rabbits at doses well above the human dose showed no evidence of teratogenicity or direct fetal harm, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Iopromide crosses the placenta in small amounts; because iodine may transiently affect the fetal/neonatal thyroid, consider neonatal thyroid evaluation after in-utero exposure.
lact: Iopromide is poorly excreted into human milk and is poorly absorbed orally by an infant. Breastfeeding can generally be continued; if a mother prefers, she may pump and discard breast milk for 12 to 24 hours after administration to minimize infant exposure.
renal: Acute kidney injury / contrast-induced nephropathy is the principal safety concern, with greatest risk in pre-existing renal impairment, diabetes, advanced vascular or cardiac disease, multiple myeloma/paraproteinemia, dehydration, advanced age, and with large or repeated doses. Iopromide is excreted essentially unchanged by the kidneys; in impairment AUC rises about 2-fold (moderate) to 6-fold (severe) and terminal half-life lengthens to about 11.6 hours. Use the lowest effective dose, hydrate before and after, avoid additional nephrotoxins, and monitor creatinine/eGFR (recheck at 48 hours when withholding metformin). Iopromide is dialyzable.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is required. Iopromide undergoes negligible hepatic metabolism and is excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney, so hepatic impairment has limited effect on its elimination. Hepatic disease is relevant mainly as a factor favoring temporary withholding of metformin around the procedure.

major: Metformin and other biguanides - acute contrast-related changes in renal function may precipitate lactic acidosis; withhold in patients with eGFR 30-60 mL/min/1.73m2 or hepatic impairment (historically held 48 hours before and after) and re-evaluate renal function at 48 hours before resuming
Beta-blockers - patients may be unresponsive to usual epinephrine doses used to treat allergic reactions and may have a lowered threshold for hypersensitivity reactions
moderate: Interleukins (e.g., IL-2) - increased prevalence of delayed hypersensitivity reactions (fever, chills, rash, pruritus, nausea, hypotension)
Other nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, cisplatin) - additive renal injury
minor: Concurrent diuretics or antihypertensives - may worsen dehydration and CIN risk if hydration is inadequate
interactions.alcohol: Not directly applicable to the agent; a history of alcoholism is one factor favoring temporary withholding of metformin around the procedure.
interactions.diagnostics: May interfere with thyroid uptake of radioactive iodine - avoid thyroid radioiodine therapy or testing for up to 6 weeks; transiently increases protein-bound iodine - defer PBI testing for at least 16 days.

serious: Cardiac arrest, ventricular fibrillation, myocardial infarction
Thromboembolic events (stroke, MI) during arterial procedures
rare: Thyroid storm in patients with thyroid autonomy
Sickling in homozygous sickle cell disease
emergency: Anaphylaxis / severe hypersensitivity with airway compromise or shock
Acute pulmonary edema or respiratory arrest
Stroke or myocardial infarction during arterial procedures

monitoring: Renal function (serum creatinine / eGFR) before and after administration, especially in at-risk patients (recheck at 48 hours when withholding metformin)
Hydration status before and after the procedure
Observation for hypersensitivity/anaphylactoid reactions for 30-60 minutes after dosing, with resuscitation equipment available
Vital signs and cardiovascular status during and after arterial procedures
Thyroid function in pediatric patients 0-3 years (especially preterm neonates and those with cardiac disease)
counsel: Tell the team about any prior reaction to contrast media, iodine, asthma, or other allergies before the procedure
Drink fluids and stay well hydrated before and after the exam to protect your kidneys
A feeling of warmth or flushing during the injection is common and brief
If you take metformin, tell the team - it may be held around the procedure and restarted after a kidney blood test in about 48 hours
Report any rash, itching, hives, swelling, or trouble breathing during or after the procedure, including delayed skin reactions over the following days
Report pain or swelling at the injection site right away - it could mean the contrast leaked into the tissue
Recent contrast can affect thyroid tests and radioactive iodine scans for several weeks - tell any provider ordering thyroid studies
pk: Immediate intravascular peak after bolus; rapid extracellular distribution (Vd ~16 L)
Main elimination half-life ~2 hours (terminal ~6.2 h); ~11.6 h in severe renal impairment
Single procedural dose; ~97% excreted unchanged in urine
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); protect from light; may warm to body temperature; discard bulk package 10 h after puncture
pearls: Do NOT administer Ultravist intrathecally - inadvertent intrathecal use can cause death, seizures, and severe neurologic injury
Contrast-induced AKI is the dominant risk - use the lowest dose, hydrate before and after, and avoid concurrent nephrotoxins
Prior contrast reaction roughly triples anaphylactoid risk; keep epinephrine and resuscitation equipment ready and observe 30-60 minutes
Beta-blocked patients may be refractory to usual epinephrine doses - consider glucagon and prepare for harder-to-treat reactions
Withhold metformin around the procedure in at-risk patients (eGFR 30-60 or hepatic impairment) and recheck renal function at 48 hours before restarting
Concentration is chosen by procedure: 370 for coronary/visceral/ventriculography, 300 for cerebral/peripheral arteriography, urography, and CT
missed: Not applicable. Iopromide is a single-use diagnostic contrast agent administered once at the time of imaging; there is no maintenance dosing schedule and therefore no missed-dose concept.
overdose: Adverse effects of overdosage are life-threatening and affect mainly the pulmonary and cardiovascular systems. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive and symptomatic, directed at the support of all vital functions. Because protein binding is negligible, iopromide is dialyzable and can be removed by hemodialysis.
